sources: Sequoia & Kings Canyon trail conditions page

trails.trailTip: Weekend and holiday visits require riding the free shuttle or arriving very early, since the Giant Forest Museum parking area fills quickly in summer.
trails.didYouKnow: The loop passes the General Sherman Tree, the largest tree on Earth by volume, along with several other named giant sequoias.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the Moro Rock staircase closes whenever ice or snow makes the granite steps unsafe, typically from late fall through spring — check current conditions before driving up.
trails.didYouKnow: The roughly 400-step granite staircase was built in the 1930s and climbs a dome that offers a 360-degree view of the Great Western Divide.

trails.trailTip: Flow is most dramatic during May and June snowmelt and can slow to a trickle by late summer, so time an early-season visit if the falls themselves are the goal.
trails.didYouKnow: Tokopah Falls tumbles roughly 1,200 feet down a granite canyon wall carved by glaciers, similar in character to Yosemite's high country.

trails.trailTip: The meadow's edges are boggy well into early summer — stay on the boardwalk sections to protect the fragile meadow soil.
trails.didYouKnow: John Muir called Crescent Meadow the 'gem of the Sierra' after visiting in the 1870s.

trails.trailTip: Snow can linger on the upper switchbacks into July, and afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, so start at dawn and turn back if lightning threatens.
trails.didYouKnow: At just under 11,200 feet, Alta Peak's summit gives one of the best views in the park of the Great Western Divide and the Kaweah watershed.

trails.trailTip: The trail can stay snowy and hard to follow into June at higher elevations — check current trail conditions before an early-season attempt.
trails.didYouKnow: Heather Lake sits in a granite bowl within the Tokopah watershed and is one of several lakes reached via the Lakes Trail system.

trails.trailTip: This low-elevation trail gets very hot in summer with little shade — it's best hiked in spring when the falls also carry the most water.
trails.didYouKnow: Marble Falls cascades over a formation of marble, a metamorphic rock unusual among the mostly granite peaks of the surrounding Sierra.

trails.trailTip: The exposed granite summit can be windy and offers little shelter — bring a layer even on a warm day.
trails.didYouKnow: From the summit, hikers can see both the Great Western Divide and, on clear days, the San Joaquin Valley to the west.

animals.whereToLook: Meadow edges and berry-producing shrubs throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Stay at least 50 yards away and never leave food or scented items unattended — bears here can be food-conditioned, and a fed bear often has to be relocated or, in repeat cases, euthanized.
animals.didYouKnow: Sequoia's black bears come in color phases ranging from black to cinnamon-brown, so coat color alone doesn't distinguish them from grizzlies, which no longer live in California.

animals.whereToLook: Crescent Meadow and other meadow edges
animals.viewingTip: In late spring and early summer, give does extra space — fawns often lie motionless and hidden nearby, and a doe may act defensively if she feels her fawn is threatened.
animals.didYouKnow: Mule deer get their name from their large, mule-like ears, which can rotate independently to track sound.

animals.whereToLook: High alpine terrain above 10,000 feet in the park's eastern reaches
animals.viewingTip: This is a federally endangered subspecies found only in a handful of Sierra herds — view any sighting through binoculars or a spotting scope from a trail or ridge, and never approach for a closer look.
animals.didYouKnow: Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep numbered under 100 individuals in the 1990s; recovery efforts have since grown the population, but it remains one of the rarest large mammals in North America.

animals.whereToLook: Mixed-conifer and giant sequoia groves at mid-elevation
animals.viewingTip: Fishers den in large tree cavities and are extremely sensitive to disturbance — if you spot one, watch quietly from a distance rather than following it toward a den tree.
animals.didYouKnow: The Sierra Nevada fisher population is genetically isolated and was proposed for federal listing due to its small, fragmented range.

animals.whereToLook: Campgrounds and trailheads throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: These jays are naturally curious around people, but resist the urge to toss them food — human food habituates them and can make them aggressive at picnic areas.
animals.didYouKnow: Steller's jays are excellent mimics and can imitate the call of a red-tailed hawk to scare other birds away from a food source.

animals.whereToLook: Giant sequoia groves, especially near cone-drop piles
animals.viewingTip: Watch these active little squirrels forage from a bench or the trail rather than offering food — a wild diet keeps them healthy and their natural behavior intact.
animals.didYouKnow: Douglas squirrels harvest and cache thousands of sequoia cones each year, and their gnawing helps release seeds — making them an important part of sequoia regeneration.

animals.viewingTip: Sightings are rare; if one occurs, keep your distance, pick up small children, and never run — back away slowly while giving the animal a clear path to leave.
animals.didYouKnow: Mountain lions in the Sierra foothills maintain some of the largest home ranges of any big cat in North America, often covering 100 square miles or more.

animals.whereToLook: High-elevation groves and rocky overlooks near Alta Peak and Little Baldy
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy this bold, gray bird at a normal trail distance and skip the temptation to hand out snacks — nutcrackers that rely on human food cache fewer of the pine seeds forests depend on.
animals.didYouKnow: A single Clark's nutcracker can cache tens of thousands of pine seeds each fall and reliably relocate them months later by memory.
